papers.title: Parasite Features: Causal Abstraction Through Spurious Pathways
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26711v1

summary.one_liner: The paper shows that Distributed Alignment Search, a causal-abstraction interpretability method, can be fooled by "parasite features": pairs of representation directions that jointly mimic a claimed algorithm without the model actually using the feature.
summary.plain: Researchers study how to tell what computation a neural network is really doing inside. One popular test checks whether a simple, human-readable algorithm matches the network's internal behavior. This paper reports that the test can be passed by a misleading pair of internal directions that only look like the intended feature, and the authors demonstrate this on syntactic agreement and two-digit addition tasks.
summary.why: It matters because interpretability claims often rest on these equivalence tests, so a method that can be spuriously satisfied could lead researchers to wrongly conclude a model uses a given feature. The text frames it as a caution for best practices rather than a claim that existing findings are wrong.
summary.background:
- Mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering what computations a neural network performs internally.
- Causal abstraction: a framework saying a network "implements" an algorithm if swapping or intervening on its internal parts behaves the same way as the algorithm.
- Distributed Alignment Search (DAS): a method that learns a linear map to find directions in a network's internal state that correspond to a high-level variable.
- Representation space: the set of internal numerical activations a network uses; a "direction" is a particular combination of those numbers.
- Spurious feature: something that passes a test for the wrong reason.

papers.abstract: Causal Abstraction defines a notion of \emph{equivalence} between a neural network and an algorithm, thus serving as a powerful framework for mechanistic interpretability. In this paper, however, we show the existence of a class of \emph{spurious features} which straightforwardly pass such equivalence tests. Suppose there are two directions in a model's representation space where: (i) one discriminates the input based on some feature, and (ii) the other steers the model towards a certain output. Interpretability methods based on Causal Abstraction (e.g., Distributed Alignment Search) can \emph{spuriously} simulate these directions' combined behavior by leveraging pathways passing through them, giving the impression that the model implements this feature. In such cases, we say the method discovered a \defn{parasite feature}. Experimentally, we show that Distributed Alignment Search finds parasite features using linear alignment maps in two tasks: syntactic agreement and two-digit addition. Our paper highlights an important consideration for Causal Abstraction and contributes to the ongoing debate about best practices for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: WaXup: Weight Averaging of Experts as Data Augmentation for Robust Introspection
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27353v1

summary.one_liner: WaXup augments the training data for trainable introspection (models trained to describe their own finetuned behaviors) by linearly interpolating weights of finetuned expert models, and reports better and more robust descriptions on three benchmarks.
summary.plain: Researchers want language models that can explain, in plain words, what they were trained to do, so people can check them for hidden or unwanted behaviors. This paper proposes WaXup, which creates extra training examples by averaging the settings (weights) of several specialized versions of a model. The authors report that this improves the accuracy and robustness of these self-descriptions on three test sets, including one built with models deliberately trained to hide their behaviors.
summary.why: As language models grow more capable, checking what they have learned is getting harder, and self-explanation is one proposed route to auditing them. The work matters for AI safety auditing, though the text alone does not show how well it would hold up on the most capable or real-world systems.
summary.background:
- Finetuning: further training a pretrained model on a specific task, producing a specialized "expert" version.
- Mechanistic interpretability: studying a model's internal workings directly, which the abstract says is struggling to keep pace with larger models.
- Trainable introspection: training a model to answer questions in natural language about what it learned during finetuning.
- Weight space and interpolation: each model is a long list of numbers (weights); averaging two such lists gives a model "in between" the two.
- Linear mode connectivity: the observed property that averaged finetuned models often keep the behaviors of the originals.
- Data augmentation: creating extra training examples to make learning more robust; MiXup is the framework this builds on.
- AuditBench: a suite of models adversarially trained to conceal their behaviors, used to test alignment auditing.

papers.abstract: As the capabilities of large language models keep improving, traditional mechanistic interpretability methods struggle to keep pace. In contrast, trainable introspection methods emerge as a promising alternative; they repurpose the model itself as a self-diagnostic tool, trained to verbalize what it has learned during finetuning in natural language. While training on datasets of finetuned experts achieves encouraging results, it currently lacks robustness and generalization. Building on the data augmentation framework of MiXup, we introduce WaXup, a method that augments the introspection training set through linear interpolation in the weight space. This is motivated by the linear mode connectivity property: weight averaged experts interpolate the behaviors of the initial experts. We evaluate WaXup on three benchmarks: hidden-behavior models, a meta-dataset of real-world NLP tasks and AuditBench, a challenging alignment auditing suite of models adversarially trained to conceal their behaviors. WaXup improves the accuracy of generated descriptions as well as robustness to various distribution shifts. We hope to improve the reliability of trainable introspection methods towards better and safer models.

papers.title: X Hedging: towards an eXplainable artificial intelligence option Hedging framework
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25870v1

summary.background:
- Hedging: taking offsetting positions so that losses in one investment are cushioned by gains in another.
- Option: a contract giving the right to buy or sell an asset at a set price later.
- Deep Hedging: an existing approach that uses neural networks (layered mathematical models learned from data) to pick hedging actions.
- Tree ensemble / LightGBM: many simple decision trees combined; often easier to inspect than neural networks.
- Reinforcement-learning style: learning a strategy by trying actions and adjusting based on outcomes.
- Explainability: how well a person can understand why a model made a choice.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes X Hedging, which replaces the neural networks in Deep Hedging with LightGBM tree ensembles trained sequentially in random orders to learn option hedging policies.
summary.plain: The paper is about how banks and traders protect ("hedge") themselves against losses on financial options, a task often handled by neural-network models that are hard to interpret and need lots of data. The authors swap those networks for a different kind of model built from many small decision trees, and report that it performs comparably in their controlled experiments. They also report it is faster to compute, more robust when data is scarce, and easier for users to understand.
summary.why: As more automated decision systems are used in finance, there is interest in models whose reasoning people can inspect, and this paper offers one concrete option. The text supports only controlled experiments, so how well the result carries over to real markets is not shown here.

papers.abstract: We propose X Hedging, an alternative to the Deep Hedging framework that addresses computational and explainability limitations of neural-network-based hedging strategies. Deep Hedging leverages neural networks to learn flexible hedging policies but relies on opaque models and typically requires large training datasets, which can complicate interpretation and limit its effectiveness in data-constrained settings. X Hedging takes a step toward addressing these limitations by replacing neural networks with tree ensemble methods, specifically LightGBM, to estimate hedging strategies. This design provides a computationally efficient alternative while preserving strong hedging performance and moving toward more user-centered explainability. To integrate LightGBM into a reinforcement-learning-style hedging framework, we introduce an optimization approach that sequentially trains tree-ensemble models while introducing stochasticity through random training orders. In controlled experiments, X Hedging achieves performance comparable to Deep Hedging while offering greater user-centered explainability, improved computational efficiency, and substantially higher robustness when training data are limited. The numerical results demonstrate that tree-ensemble methods provide an effective computational alternative to neural networks for data-driven dynamic hedging.

papers.title: Explainable AI for Solar PV Power Forecasting: From Model Selection to Trustworthy, Reproducible Deployment
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25894v1

summary.background:
- Solar PV forecasting: predicting a plant's power output from weather data, often a day ahead.
- Numerical weather prediction (NWP): computer weather forecasts on a grid; here, cells 4 km across.
- nRMSE: root mean square error divided by installed capacity, so errors are comparable across plants.
- Smart persistence: a simple baseline that assumes tomorrow looks like today at the same time, adjusted for clear-sky output.
- Random vs. time-based validation: shuffled splits can leak information from the future and look too good.
- SHAP: a method that scores how much each input feature pushes a prediction up or down.
- Conformal calibration: a statistical adjustment that makes stated prediction intervals match observed coverage (here, 80% nominal coverage rose from 64.5% to 81.7%).
- Edge hardware: small local devices running models instead of cloud servers.
summary.one_liner: A review plus a reproducible workflow that pairs automated model search with explainable AI (SHAP attributions and conformal prediction intervals) for one-day-ahead solar PV power forecasting, tested on a 16.32 kWp plant in Porto, Portugal.
summary.plain: This paper is about predicting how much electricity a small rooftop-scale solar plant will produce the next day, using machine learning models fed with weather forecasts. The authors review the main kinds of models used for this and then test a step-by-step workflow on one openly available dataset. They report that the choice of input features mattered much more than the choice among strong algorithms, and that their prediction intervals only became reliable after a calibration step.
summary.why: Solar forecasts feed into grid planning and electricity trading, so trustworthy error estimates matter, and the paper's emphasis on comparable benchmarks and honest validation addresses a real problem in the field. The results come from a single small plant and one dataset, so they show what happened there rather than a general rule.

papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) is now a standard tool for forecasting the output of solar photovoltaic (PV) plants, yet published accuracy figures are often hard to compare and harder to trust. Many studies validate with random splits, report no reference forecast, and present feature attributions without saying what they can and cannot show. This paper reviews the main families of ML methods for PV power forecasting and resource assessment, from tree ensembles to deep and foundation models, and sets out a reproducible workflow that combines automated model search with explainable AI. The workflow is then tested on an openly available dataset: a 16.32 kWp plant in Porto, Portugal, forecast one day ahead from a 4 km numerical weather prediction grid. Over a full test year, the best models reach a normalised root mean square error (nRMSE) of 11.6% of installed capacity, about half the error of smart persistence. The choice of input features changed accuracy far more than the choice among strong algorithms, and shuffled cross-validation was mildly optimistic. After conformal calibration, the nominal 80% prediction intervals covered 81.7% of observations, against 64.5% before. SHAP rankings stayed stable when the model was retrained on different periods but shifted when correlated inputs were removed, so attributions should be read as properties of a model rather than of the plant. The paper closes with practical lessons and open problems, including deployment on edge hardware and the effect of a changing climate.

papers.title: Separating Interpretability and Reconstruction in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25165v1

summary.background:
- Neural network representation: the numerical internal signals a model uses for an input such as an image or sentence.
- Autoencoder: a model that compresses an input into a code and then tries to rebuild the original from that code.
- Sparse autoencoder (SAE): an autoencoder that forces only a few code entries to be active at once, so each entry tends to correspond to a distinct idea.
- Reconstruction fidelity: how closely the rebuilt signal matches the original.
- Monosemanticity: a score for whether a code feature corresponds to one clear concept rather than several mixed ones.
- Decorrelation loss: a training penalty that discourages two outputs from carrying the same information.
- Steering: nudging a model's behavior by adjusting its internal features.
summary.one_liner: DualSAE augments a standard sparse autoencoder with a plug-in Residual Branch, decorrelated from a Sparse Branch, so that interpretability and reconstruction fidelity are handled by separate components.
summary.plain: Researchers study how to break a neural network's internal signals into simple, human-readable pieces. A common tool does this with one set of pieces that must both explain the signal accurately and be easy to interpret, but those two goals may pull against each other. The paper proposes splitting the job into two parts: one part keeps the main meaning, and a second part captures the leftover details, with a penalty that keeps the two parts from overlapping.
summary.why: The paper reports gains in reconstruction accuracy (about 29%) and in a measure of interpretability called monosemanticity (about 34%) across vision and language tests, plus improvements in topic modeling, hypothesis generation, and steering a language model. These are the authors' own reported averages from the abstract, and the text does not show how robust they are beyond those experiments. It may matter for efforts to understand what large AI models represent internally.

papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are effective tools for mechanistic interpretability by decomposing neural representations into sparse and interpretable features. However, a single sparse representation in traditional SAEs is responsible for both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability, which are not guaranteed to align. To separate these objectives, we propose DualSAE, a modular framework that augments standard SAEs with a plug-in Residual Branch. A standard SAE serves as the Sparse Branch, learning a sparse code that contains the dominant semantics of the input. The added Residual Branch models the non-semantic information omitted by the Sparse Branch. We ensure that the contributions of the two branches towards the overall reconstruction have minimal overlap through a decorrelation loss. We also adopt a two-stage training strategy that first stabilizes sparse representation learning before coupling with the Residual Branch. Across diverse encoder-SAE configurations on two vision datasets and two language corpora, DualSAE achieves mean relative improvements of approximately 29% in reconstruction fidelity and 34% in interpretability (measured by monosemanticity score). Moreover, with more interpretable representations, DualSAE yields consistent performance gains in the downstream applications of topic modeling, hypothesis generation, and LLM steering. Qualitative analysis further suggests that the Sparse Branch indeed preserves dominant semantic content, whereas the Residual Branch captures non-semantic information to improve reconstruction fidelity.

papers.title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24619v1

summary.background:
- Activation probe: a small classifier trained on a model's internal numbers (activations) to detect a property, such as unsafe output.
- Sparse autoencoder (SAE): a tool that re-expresses internal activations as a larger set of sparse features, many of which can be interpreted by humans.
- Boolean logic / logic gates: rules built from AND, OR and NOT on yes/no inputs; here, SAE features are first turned into on/off values.
- Gate budget: a limit on how many logic gates a rule may use, keeping it small and interpretable.
- KV cache: memory a language model keeps for previously processed tokens; losing capacity to monitors reduces serving efficiency.
- vLLM: a widely used open-source system for serving language models efficiently.
summary.one_liner: GateWatch is a compact monitor for LLM activations that expresses its decision as Boolean logic over a few binarized sparse-autoencoder features, and is evaluated on 24 tasks with Gemma-2-9B and inside vLLM serving.
summary.plain: Large language models are increasingly used in agents, and developers want cheap ways to spot unsafe or unintended behavior while the model runs. This paper proposes GateWatch, a small classifier that makes its yes/no decision with simple AND/OR/NOT-style rules over a handful of readable internal features of the model. On 24 tasks with Gemma-2-9B, the authors report about 80.5% mean test accuracy using roughly 4 features and 3.5 logic gates per probe, about 1.2 points below probes that use all 16K features, while cutting probe memory by 99.98%.
summary.why: Monitoring that is both cheap and human-readable could matter for safety checks on deployed models, since the decision rule can be inspected rather than being a black box. The text reports serving results inside vLLM (97-98% of baseline throughput with 1,000 concurrent classifiers), but the evaluation is limited to one model family and the paper's own tasks, so how well it generalizes is not established here.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, multi-token GateWatch classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.

papers.title: Tracking Representations in LLM Reasoning Traces for Iterated Games
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23403v1

summary.background:
- Chain-of-thought (CoT): a model writing out intermediate reasoning steps as text before its final answer.
- Mechanistic interpretability: analyzing the model's internal numerical activations (per layer) to see what information is represented and when.
- Iterated games with incomplete information: repeated strategic interactions where players cannot see everything, such as hidden states or opponents' intentions.
- Multi-agent systems: setups where several AI agents interact with one another.
- Belief/representation: the model's internal working picture of the game state, which the paper tracks across reasoning steps.
summary.one_liner: Mechanistic interpretability study showing that LLM agents in iterated games with incomplete information form, revise, and sometimes prematurely lock in an internal game representation during chain-of-thought, with the failure visible in both the text trace and layer activations.
summary.plain: Language-model agents often "think out loud" before making a decision, but it is unclear whether that written reasoning matches what the model is really computing. The authors studied agents playing repeated games where some information is hidden, and used interpretability tools that look inside the network. They report that the model builds and keeps revising its picture of the game as it reasons, and that once it commits too early to a wrong belief, it rarely recovers.
summary.why: As language-model agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings, a way to pinpoint where strategic reasoning goes wrong could make those failures easier to diagnose. The text does not establish how far the findings generalize beyond the games studied, so that remains an open question.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents achieve state-of-the-art performance across domains through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Despite their ubiquitous use, little is understood about the relationship between the externalized trace and the model's actual computation. We address this by investigating how LLM agents make decisions in iterative games with incomplete information. Using a series of mechanistic interpretability techniques, we find that the model forms and iteratively revises an internal representation of the game throughout the CoT. Once the model prematurely commits to an incorrect belief, it rarely recovers. This failure is manifested in both the literal trace and the layer activations. Ultimately, as multi-agent systems are more prevalent, our work opens the door to a more focused diagnosis of their strategic reasoning errors. For illustrative purposes, we offer an interactive visualizer of our methodology on selected sample traces at https://interp-self.github.io/gametrace/

papers.title: Right Labels, Wrong Reasons: Signed Feature Attribution for Multi-Label Explainability
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22515v1

summary.background:
- Multi-label classification: each item can carry several tags at once (e.g., a photo labelled both "beach" and "sunset").
- Black-box model: a model whose internal workings are hard to inspect directly.
- Global surrogate: a simpler, interpretable model trained to imitate a complex model's outputs across a whole dataset.
- Fisher LDA (linear discriminant analysis): a classic method that finds a weighted combination of features that best separates two groups; its weights act as feature importances.
- Fidelity: how closely the surrogate's predictions match the original model's.
- Binary Relevance: a common baseline that handles each label as a separate yes/no problem.
summary.one_liner: FLEX, a global surrogate built on a single multi-label Fisher LDA, yields signed per-label feature attribution lists that approximate black-box multi-label classifiers and flags labels whose separability may be weak.
summary.plain: Machine-learning models that tag items with several labels at once can be right for the wrong reasons, and it is hard to see why they decide what they do. This paper proposes a simpler stand-in model, FLEX, that copies the original classifier's predictions and lists which input features push each label up or down. The text reports that it reproduces the original predictions with high fidelity across the benchmarks and classifier types tested.
summary.why: Explanations that show which features drive each label could help people check whether a multi-label system is reasoning sensibly before trusting it. The abstract's claims rest on its own evaluations, which I could not check, so the strength of the results is unverified.

papers.abstract: When a multi-label classifier assigns the right labels, it may do so for the wrong reasons. Diffuse feature combinations may vary across classifier families and lack a dominant feature. This paper proposes FLEX (Fisher LDA Explainer), a global surrogate that fits a single direct multi-label Fisher LDA over the full binary label matrix, producing signed feature attribution lists for each label in a single coherent coordinate system. Across the evaluated benchmarks and classifier families, FLEX reproduces the black box's predictions with consistently high fidelity. Pooling covariance across labels outperforms a per-label alternative on most datasets, with the advantage growing largest where labels are numerous and positive examples are scarce. FLEX's fidelity-complexity Pareto curve is monotonically increasing, giving practitioners a predictable path to higher-fidelity explanations as more features are used, and its in-sample fidelity matches or leads Binary Relevance alternatives once a modest feature budget is allowed. The magnitude of each discriminant weight vector bounds its label's separability, flagging labels that may be predicted correctly for the wrong reasons. The evaluated classifiers largely agree on which predictions to make, but reach those decisions through different feature subsets when no single feature dominates.

papers.title: Can Mechanistic Interpretability Help Explain LLM Agent Failures? A Case Study on Web Element Hallucination
papers.label: arXiv:2611.18514v1

summary.one_liner: A case study applying mechanistic interpretability tools (linear probes, activation steering, circuit analysis) to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct web agents that hallucinate actions unavailable on live websites, and reporting where these tools succeed and where they fall short.
summary.plain: Web agents are AI systems that click and type on websites, and sometimes they try to use a button or option that isn't actually on the page. The authors looked inside a 7-billion-parameter language model while it browsed live sites to see whether this mistake could be spotted and corrected from its internal signals. A simple probe could flag likely hallucinations before the model writes its action (AUC 0.80), and nudging the model along that direction fixed 85% of them, though it also broke 7% of actions that were already correct.
summary.why:
The paper is a candid test of whether interpretability methods that work on language models in general can explain real agent failures; its mixed results point to where current methods need to change. It is a single model and a single failure type, so the findings are best read as a case study rather than a general answer.</await>
<parameter name="background">- Large language model (LLM): a neural network trained on text that generates responses token by token.
- Mechanistic interpretability: studying the internal numerical signals of a model to work out which parts compute what.
- Linear probe: a simple classifier trained on a model's internal activations to predict some property, here whether a hallucination is coming.
- AUC (area under the ROC curve): a 0 to 1 score of how well a classifier separates two outcomes; 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect.
- Activation steering: adding a learned direction to internal activations to push the model's behavior one way.
- Circuit: a subset of model components and positions that jointly carry out a computation.
- Hallucination (in agents): choosing an action that does not exist in the current environment.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">research-level

papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has made significant progress in explaining the internal computations of Large Language Models (LLMs); however, these advances have yet to demonstrate comparable success in explaining the decision-making processes of LLM-based agents. This paper examines the challenges MI tools face when applied to realistic agentic failures. We focus on one such failure: web agents hallucinating actions that are not available on a website. We apply a series of mechanistic analyzes to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as it interacts with live websites. We find that a linear probe trained on the last prompt token can predict hallucinations before generation begins (0.80 AUC) and steering along a probe direction corrects 85\% of hallucinations, but disrupts 7\% of valid actions. However, these results only provide a partial explanation of why the agent hallucinates. The probe direction is sensitive to prompt formatting, losing much of its steering effect after a minor change to how actions are represented. Additionally, circuit identification can be difficult as the computation is distributed across multiple components and positions, and the information the agent relies on varies across examples. We discuss how these observations challenge the assumptions underlying standard MI methods for circuit discovery and feature identification, and outline future directions for making these methods better suited to explain failures in LLM-based agents.

papers.title: DECODE: Diagnosing Interpretability Failures in Automated Interpretation Process
papers.label: arXiv:2611.17856v1

summary.background:
- Large Language Models (LLMs): AI systems trained on large amounts of text.
- Interpretability: the effort to understand what happens inside an AI model, such as which internal signals stand for which concepts.
- Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features: a method that splits a model's internal activity into many separate, roughly meaningful signals, each of which can be described in words.
- Automated interpretation: using an LLM to write a plain-language description of each signal and to score how well that description fits.
- Ground truth: a known correct answer to check against; here it is missing, which makes validation hard.
- Inter-coder consensus: in qualitative research, agreement between independent human coders used as a sign of reliability; this paper borrows the idea by comparing independently generated explanations.
- Visual analytics: software that uses interactive charts and views so people can explore data and judge results.
summary.one_liner: DECODE is a visual analytics system that adds human review to an LLM-driven pipeline for interpreting Sparse Autoencoder features, using inter-explanation consensus as a reliability proxy and an active seeding protocol to pick instances for manual inspection.
summary.plain: Researchers often use AI language models both to explain the internal workings of other AI models and to grade those explanations, with little human checking. This paper presents a tool called DECODE that brings people back into that loop, helping them tell whether a bad explanation comes from the extracted internal features or from the language model doing the explaining. The authors report a case study on 16,384 features, and say the approach can find and attribute failures at scale.
summary.why: Automated explanations of AI internals are increasingly used without ground truth to check them, so a method for locating where errors come from may matter for trusting such tools. The text does not show how well the approach works beyond its single case study, so its broader value is unclear.

papers.abstract: Tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on LLMs themselves to both generate and evaluate explanations, creating a self-referential automated interpretation process with minimal human oversight. This automation raises significant reliability concerns, which are exacerbated by the absence of ground truth. In practice, it is difficult to validate explanations or to attribute interpretability failures to their source -- whether they originate from the tool's extracted representations or from the LLM used in the process. To address these challenges, we present DECODE, a visual analytics system that reintroduces human oversight into the automated interpretation process. Our approach decomposes the diagnostic workflow into three progressive stages, isolating failure sources ranging from structural defects to explanation-level misalignments. Drawing inspiration from inter-coder consensus in qualitative analysis, we utilize consensus among independently generated explanations and their evaluation metrics as a proxy for reliability. To further scale human inspection, we employ a three-phase active seeding protocol that strategically recommends high-priority instances for manual review. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a case study on 16,384 Sparse Autoencoder features, showing that it can efficiently identify and attribute interpretability failures at scale.
